title: Chapter 3: The Rise of the Student Leader
keywords: National Union of Students of the Philippines
primary_topics: Chapter 3 covers Dayunior/Art's three-year FEU undergraduate period (1955-1958) -- the place he had not chosen becoming the pivot of his life, both through accidental academic excellence (graduating Associate in Arts 'With Highest Honors' = summa cum laude) and through the unprecedented student-leader trajectory that ran from freshman delegate to FEUCSO President during his sophomore year of law school.

The faith awakening of a 'Catholic ignoramus': Fr. Michael Nolan SSC (Columban priest, archdiocesan SCA spiritual director, FEU university chaplain) and the SCA bloc deliver swing votes to Art, then Fr. Nolan reciprocates by teaching the un-catechized FEUCSO president the basics of his religion -- only three prayers (Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be), invitations to special Masses, and 'a few booklets about Catholicism, not even a book.' The Irish priest who 'taught by example more than by words' becomes the second great mentor of CJP's life.

The political pivots of student leadership 1957-1958: the recount-by-five-votes Law Institute chairmanship win (the first time a sophomore had ever won it), then the unprecedented FEUCSO presidency over the chairman of the College of Commerce delegation; CJP's refusal of the SCAP Vice-Presidency for International Affairs that would have taken him to Peking and Moscow; and the founding walkout from SCAP and CONDA, framed at the time as a rejection of both communist infiltration and government overreach.

The 1957 founding of the National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP) -- co-founded with Fr. Nolan, in concert with Fr. John Delaney SJ at UPSCA, initially uniting 17 schools (UP, FEU, San Beda, St. Theresa's, others), eventually drawing Ateneo, La Salle, Maryknoll, Holy Spirit, St. Scholastica's, USC Cebu, and USA Iloilo. CJP as founding president; the NUSP's mission articulated as 'to unite and reflect faithfully student opinion ... to free the student from undue political interference, to fight communist infiltration on the campuses, and to redirect the youth's thinking and energy towards constructive idealism.'

Two losses bracketing the chapter: the death of Artemio Sr. ('Temi') on the morning of February 17, 1955, at the UST Hospital ER -- five hours of waiting as the nurses bypassed him, asthma attack untreated, Temi expiring just as the dean of the UST College of Medicine arrived; the loss that made the filial law-career vow irrevocable. And the absence of any other family safety net that would shape Art's reliance on Fr. Nolan.

stances.claim: FEU was the institutional accident that was actually providential -- Art initially unhappy at not getting UP or UST, but the place he had not chosen brought him to Fr. Nolan and the SCA; his 2002 commencement claim that 'going to this university proved to be one of the best turns of my entire life' is the chapter's verdict.

stances.claim: The bypass of Temi in the UST Hospital ER, and his death after five hours of waiting, is one of the cardinal moments of CJP's life -- the inequality 'seared into his core' and laid the foundation for the substantial-justice-for-the-poor jurisprudence he would later develop on the Bench.

stances.claim: Fr. Michael Nolan SSC was the decisive mentor of Art's young manhood -- not for what he imposed but for what he restrained: never demanded Mass attendance, taught only three prayers, gave booklets not books, 'taught by example more than by words.' The chapter argues that the minimum-imposition method was exactly what worked on a 'Catholic ignoramus' with a 'reformist streak.'
stances.rhetorical_move: pedagogical-restraint thesis; the soft mentor as the effective mentor

stances.claim: Communism was a live attraction, not a hypothetical: Art 'could have joined the extremist groups' -- the rage at Temi's bypass, the poverty, the Luis Taruc letters from his father's friend, Prof. Tongco's persuasive arguments all pointed that way. one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 covers Art's three-year FEU undergraduate stretch (1955-1958), framed by the chapter's epigraph from 1 Timothy 4:12 ('Do not let anyone look down upon you because you are young'). Initially unhappy at the place he had not chosen, Art discovers stimulating professors and discovers he can compete with UP, Ateneo and La Salle students -- and so begins the accidental triumph of FEU, the institution Quezon called 'the best non-sectarian institution in the country.' He supports himself selling Douay-Rheims Bibles (70 pesos each, ~20,000 in 2021 money) to FEU's president, treasurer and devout-Catholic professors, and reselling textbooks to classmates for free copies. On February 17, 1955, walking home from FEU, he catches sight of his asthmatic father being carried down to a taxi -- and then spends five hours in the UST Hospital ER as nurses and doctors bypass them, until the Dean of the UST College of Medicine arrives too late and Artemio Sr. expires at 54. The bypass in the ER sears into Art's core -- an inequality witnessed that the biography presents as the origin of CJP's later 'last sanctuary of the oppressed' jurisprudence. Grief and rage make communism a real attraction -- Karl Marx's tenets seeping into FEU through Prof. Primo Tongco, Jose Ma. Sison and Satur Ocampo leading the extreme left, Luis Taruc (the Hukbalahap leader who had been Temi's friend) writing Art encouraging letters from his hiding place. But another father redirects him: Father Michael Nolan SSC, the Columban Irish priest and FEU chaplain who was archdiocesan spiritual director of the Student Catholic Action. After Art is recruited as freshman delegate in the Institute of Arts and Sciences (1955) and graduates summa, he moves to the Institute of Law (1957) and is once again recruited -- this time by Fr. Nolan and outgoing FEUCSO president Ronaldo 'Rocky' Balboa -- to contend for freshman delegate and then for the chairmanship of the Law Institute. He wins the chairmanship by a five-vote recount margin (initially short by two), the first sophomore ever to hold it; then, in an unprecedented upset, the 10 SCA delegates' swing votes deliver him the FEUCSO presidency over the College of Commerce chairman. As FEUCSO president he faces two adversaries at once: communist infiltration via SCAP and CONDA (with their Peking and Moscow training trips offered to the VP for International Affairs post he is offered and refuses), and government overreach via Carlos P. Garcia's Consultative Council of Students. He responds with the first major-organization student walkout in Philippine history, leading delegates from UP, UST, San Beda, St. Theresa's, National University and Sta. Isabel out of the SCAP convention; then, with Fr. Nolan and Fr. John Delaney SJ at UPSCA, he co-founds the National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP) in 1957 with an initial roster of 17 schools, later persuading Ateneo, La Salle, Maryknoll, Holy Spirit, St. Scholastica's, USC Cebu and USA Iloilo to leave their 'sheltered cocoons' and join. The founding NUSP mission -- to free students from political interference, fight communist infiltration, and redirect youth energy toward 'constructive idealism' -- would be the doctrinal armature of much of Art's later public life. And throughout, Fr. Nolan catechizes the 'Catholic ignoramus' by minimum imposition: three prayers (Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be), booklets not books, never demanding Mass attendance, 'taught by example more than by words.' Art will say at FEU's commencement in 2002 that the place he had not chosen 'proved to be one of the best turns of my entire life.'
